chunks: "There are two big buckets: winding loss and core loss. Winding loss is the copper resistance.
The DC part is the current squared times the DC resistance, so a 3 amp load through 20 milliohms is 0. 18 watts.

On top of that, AC currents, like the ripple in a buck converter, see a higher resistance because of skin effect, where the current crowds toward the surface of the wire, and proximity effect, where neighboring turns' fields push current around.
That AC resistance can be several times the DC value at hundreds of kilohertz. Core loss comes from the magnetic material being driven around its B-H loop every cycle.
Hysteresis loss is the energy per cycle, proportional to the loop area, so it scales with frequency.

Eddy currents are circulating currents induced in the core by the changing flux, which scale roughly as frequency squared times flux squared, and are suppressed by using an insulating ferrite, laminations or powder.
We summarize it with the Steinmetz equation: P equals k f to the alpha B to the beta, with alpha around 1 to 2 and beta around 2 to 3.
So flux swing matters a lot: halving it cuts loss by around 5 times.
There are also smaller ones: fringing flux around an air gap induces eddy currents in nearby windings, and the winding capacitance causes dielectric loss and resonance at high frequency.
In a converter, DC copper loss usually dominates at low ripple, and core loss and AC copper loss grow with ripple and frequency, so you balance them in the design."
